title: Exaptation of an evolutionary constraint enables behavioural control over the composition of secreted venom in giant centipedes
projectDescription: Venoms are biochemical arsenals that have emerged in numerous animal lineages, where they have coevolved with morphological and behavioural traits for venom production and delivery. In centipedes, venom evolution is thought to be constrained by the morphological complexity of their venom glands due to physiological limitations on the number of toxins produced by their secretory cells. Here, we show that the uneven toxin expression that results from these limitations have enabled giant centipedes to regulate the composition of their secreted venom despite having morphologically undifferentiated venom glands. We show that this control is likely achieved by the complex neuronal networks that innervate each venom gland subunit and is facilitated by morphological adaptations that circumvent the physiological evolutionary constraints on venom production. Our results suggest behavioural control over venom composition may be an overlooked aspect of venom biology and provide an example of how exaptation can facilitate evolutionary innovation and novelty.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Crude secreted venom and gel-fractions from Scolopendra morsitans—venom was collected using two different milking techniques (electrostimulation and defensive milking), venoms were then seperated vie SDS-PAGE (reduced and non-reduced—, as well as venom proteins from venom glands after different venom use (full glands, after predation, after defensive milking) were analysed using LC-MS/MS. From each sample, one out of two aliquots was reduced, alkylated and trypsin digested. For LC-MS/MS, samples were separated on a Shimadzu (Japan) Nexera uHPLC with an Agilent Zorbax stable-bond C18 column (2.1 x 100 mm; particle size, 1.8 m; pore size, 300 Å), using a flow rate of 180 L/min and a gradient of 1–40 % solvent B (90 % ACN [vol/vol] and 0.1 % FA [vol/vol]) in 0.1 % FA over 25 min and 40–80 % solvent B over 4 min, and analyzed on an AB Sciex 5600 TripleTOF mass spectrometer equipped with a Turbo-V source heated to 550 °C. MS survey scans were acquired at 300 to 1800 m/z over 250 ms, and the 20 most intense ions with a charge of +2 to +5 and an intensity of at least 120 counts were selected for MS/MS. The unit mass precursor ion inclusion window mass within 0.7 Da and isotopes within 2 Da were excluded from MS/MS, with scans acquired at 80 to 1400 m/z over 100 ms and optimized for high resolution.
dataProcessingProtocol: The resulting spectra were searched with ProteinPilot version 5.0 (ABSciex) against an amino acid sequence database containing the previously published venom gland transcriptomes of S. morsitans (Undheim et al. 2014) and a list of common contaminant proteins. We used a thorough search to allow for biological modifications and amino acid substitutions and a decoy-based false discovery rate analysis to identify appropriate protein identification confidence thresholds. Proteins were ranked according to confidence score, and proteins with a rank corresponding to the highest of either a local false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 1 % or with two or more high confidence tryptic peptide matches were retained. The exception was where the lowest ranked hit was above the FDR threshold and the single high-confidence peptide hit corresponded to  >30 % of the mature toxin. For comparing differences between treatments, we used the TOP 3 method of protein quantitation to estimate the relative abundances of each venom protein across our whole venom shotgun LC-MS/MS analyses. The three most intense unique tryptic peptides (confidence > 95 %, local FDR <1) assigned to each protein were extracted from Protein Pilot peptide summaries using a custom script, and their mean area was normalised as parts per million against the total area of all means for each sample. Principal component analyses were done in R version 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) using the prcomp function and visualised using the autoplot function in the ggfortify R-package.
